questions.q: A serious play in which a person of high estate falls from prosperity to misery largely through fate or a fatal flaw is called...
questions.explanation: A tragedy centres on a serious downfall, often of a person of high status, brought about by fate, error or a tragic flaw. A farce is comic and improbable, a comedy of manners satirises social behaviour, and a chronicle play dramatises historical events, so they do not fit the definition.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The nurse's smile was a lamp in the crowded ward,' the figure of speech used is...
questions.explanation: The sentence directly identifies the smile as a lamp without using 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor. A simile would make the comparison explicit with 'like' or 'as', and personification would give human qualities to a non-human thing.

questions.q: After spending the family's last naira on a generator, Musa says, 'At least we now have light to save money by.' His statement is an example of...
questions.explanation: Musa's words imply the opposite of the situation: buying the generator has cost the family money rather than helped them save. Verbal irony occurs when the intended meaning contrasts with the literal words; a euphemism would soften a harsh fact, and a simile would make an explicit comparison.

questions.passage: By the time the Danladi family reached their new flat in Kubwa, the harmattan had already powdered the windows with dust. Mama set down the last jerrycan and, for a moment, none of them spoke. From the balcony, Sani could see a woman selling akara under a mango tree; her basin seemed to glow in the morning haze. Then Baba laughed—too loudly, Sani thought—and declared that the house was better than the one they had left in Makurdi. Sani remembered the leaking roof of that old house and the naira notes his mother had counted again and again for rent. He said nothing, but he knew the new flat had already begun to ask for more money in its own silent way.
questions.q: The point of view from which the extract is told is best described as...
questions.explanation: The narrator uses third-person pronouns but gives access mainly to Sani's thoughts, as in 'too loudly, Sani thought' and 'he knew'. First-person narration would use 'I', while omniscient narration would freely reveal the inner thoughts of all the characters.

questions.passage: By the time the Danladi family reached their new flat in Kubwa, the harmattan had already powdered the windows with dust. Mama set down the last jerrycan and, for a moment, none of them spoke. From the balcony, Sani could see a woman selling akara under a mango tree; her basin seemed to glow in the morning haze. Sani remembered the leaking roof of that old house and the naira notes his mother had counted again and again for rent. He said nothing, but he knew the new flat had already begun to ask for more money in its own silent way.
questions.q: The reference to the leaking roof and the rent money counted in the old house mainly functions as...
options: a direct address to the reader by the narrator
a comic aside that relieves the family's tension
a foreshadowing of Baba's success in Kubwa
a flashback that explains Sani's anxiety about money
questions.explanation: The narrative briefly moves from the present move to an earlier home, supplying the memory that shapes Sani's worry about expenses. This is a flashback; it does not speak directly to the reader, nor does it mainly provide comic relief.

questions.passage:
The Night Nurse

At midnight the ward is a quiet sea,
and she moves between beds with a torch for a star.
The drip counts seconds down the corridor;
a patient's cough folds the darkness, then lets it be.

Her shoes print small moons on the polished floor.
She checks the chart, the pulse, the rising line,
and turns a pillow as one would turn a prayer.
Outside, the generator coughs, then sleeps.

By dawn her eyes are two lamps burned low,
yet when the first tray rattles at the door
she straightens the sheets and calls each name
as if morning itself had come to ask for water.
questions.q: The image 'a torch for a star' chiefly presents the nurse as...
options: a person confused by the ward's darkness
a small but steady guide for patients in the dark ward
a worker afraid of the night
a figure who looks down on the patients
questions.explanation: The torch in darkness suggests guidance, and 'a star' makes that guidance seem small yet reliable. The poem does not show her as fearful, contemptuous or confused; it presents her movement as purposeful care.

questions.q: The phrase 'her eyes are two lamps burned low' most nearly suggests that the nurse is...
options: unable to see the patients clearly
questions.explanation: Lamps 'burned low' imply that her energy has been used up during the night, yet they are still lamps, so her attention and care remain. The phrase does not indicate resentment, freshness or actual blindness.

questions.q: The overall tone of the poem is best described as...
questions.explanation: The descriptions of the nurse's quiet work, her exhaustion and her care at dawn show respect and warmth. A bitter, mocking or coldly clinical tone would not fit lines that present her turning a pillow 'as one would turn a prayer'.

questions.passage: At harvest time in Umuahia, Ngozi helped her grandmother sort yam tubers in the old barn. Behind the last shelf, her hand touched a small wooden box wrapped in faded cloth. Inside lay a school exercise book marked 'Ada, 1987' and a crumpled ten-naira note. Her grandmother's hand trembled as she stared at the book. 'Your mother was saving for a sewing machine,' she whispered. On the first page, in faded ink, Ngozi read: 'For the farm that will buy my freedom.' Outside, the harmattan wind rattled the rusty roof.
questions.q: The discovery of the exercise book and the ten-naira note mainly serves to
options: suggest that the grandmother has lost her memory
reveal a hidden chapter in the mother's past
introduce a quarrel over the sharing of the yam harvest
show that Ngozi dislikes working in the barn
questions.explanation: The objects lead the grandmother to recall Ada's savings for a sewing machine, so they uncover a concealed part of family history. They do not start a quarrel over the harvest, and Ngozi's dislike of barn work is not the focus.

questions.passage: At harvest time in Umuahia, Ngozi helped her grandmother sort yam tubers in the old barn. Behind the last shelf, her hand touched a small wooden box wrapped in faded cloth. Inside lay a school exercise book marked 'Ada, 1987' and a crumpled ten-naira note. Her grandmother's hand trembled as she stared at the book. 'Your mother was saving for a sewing machine,' she whispered. On the first page, in faded ink, Ngozi read: 'For the farm that will buy my freedom.' Outside, the harmattan wind rattled the rusty roof.
questions.q: The grandmother's trembling hand chiefly conveys her
options: weakness caused by the harmattan wind
fear that Ngozi will steal the money
emotional shock at an unexpected memory
annoyance at being disturbed during work
questions.explanation: The trembling begins as she stares at the exercise book and recalls the mother's plan, so it signals powerful surprise and memory. Nothing in the passage links it to theft, annoyance, or the harmattan wind.

questions.passage: At harvest time in Umuahia, Ngozi helped her grandmother sort yam tubers in the old barn. Behind the last shelf, her hand touched a small wooden box wrapped in faded cloth. Inside lay a school exercise book marked 'Ada, 1987' and a crumpled ten-naira note. Her grandmother's hand trembled as she stared at the book. 'Your mother was saving for a sewing machine,' she whispered. On the first page, in faded ink, Ngozi read: 'For the farm that will buy my freedom.' Outside, the harmattan wind rattled the rusty roof.
questions.q: The inscription 'For the farm that will buy my freedom' chiefly suggests that the mother regarded the farm as
options: a punishment she hoped to escape at once
a place where money could never be saved
a means of earning money for a desired independence
a duty more important than her own plans
questions.explanation: The words present the farm as the source of money that would purchase freedom, not as an immediate punishment. This reading fits the discovery of the ten-naira note and the plan for a sewing machine.

questions.passage:
The farmers rise before the sun,
And work until the day is done,
And plant the maize in even row,
And watch the early seedlings grow.

The children fetch the water near,
And sing to keep away the fear,
And stack the maize in even rows,
And thank the cloud that softly blows.
questions.q: The rhyme scheme of each stanza is best described as
questions.explanation: The first two lines rhyme with each other, as in 'sun' and 'done', and the last two rhyme with each other, as in 'row' and 'grow'. This makes a paired rhyme pattern rather than alternating rhyme.

questions.passage:
The farmers rise before the sun,
And work until the day is done,
And plant the maize in even row,
And watch the early seedlings grow.

The children fetch the water near,
And sing to keep away the fear,
And stack the maize in even rows,
And thank the cloud that softly blows.
questions.q: The repetition of 'And' at the beginning of the second, third and fourth lines is best described as
questions.explanation: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines or clauses. A refrain is a repeated line or group of lines, a caesura is a pause within a line, and enjambment is a run-on line.

questions.q: In many African oral performances, the audience's answer to the lead performer's call mainly serves to
options: correct the performer's errors before the next episode
affirm participation and sustain the rhythm of the performance
prove that the story has already been written down
signal that the performance should end at once
questions.explanation: Call-and-response makes the audience active co-performers, confirming involvement and helping to pace the performance. It is not chiefly a correction device, an ending signal, or proof of written composition.

questions.q: In a play, when the audience knows that the letter in the hero's pocket will ruin him but the hero does not, the technique used is
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows more than a character does about the situation. Verbal irony involves saying the opposite of what is meant, situational irony is a contrast between expectation and outcome, and a pun is wordplay.

questions.q: A play uses a group of villagers who chant together and comment on the action, representing the voice of the community. This dramatic convention is known as
questions.explanation: A chorus is a group that speaks or chants together and comments on the action, often representing communal opinion. An aside is a brief private remark to the audience, a soliloquy is a character's solitary speech, and comic relief is a humorous break in a serious play.

questions.q: In the expression 'Mama Bose's stall is a small kingdom of bananas and groundnuts,' the figure of speech used is
questions.explanation: The stall is directly described as a kingdom without using 'like' or 'as', so the comparison is a metaphor. It is not a simile, and no name of an object is substituted for something closely associated with it.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The palm wine gurgled into the calabash and the lid clattered on the bench,' the figure of speech used is
questions.explanation: Words such as 'gurgled' and 'clattered' imitate or suggest the sounds they describe, which is onomatopoeia. No human quality is given to an object, no comparison uses 'like' or 'as', and there is no contradictory pairing.

questions.q: The sentence 'The trader carried a bag of garri that weighed a ton and still balanced a basin of fish on her head' contains an example of
questions.explanation: The statement deliberately exaggerates the weight of the bag as 'a ton' for emphasis, which is hyperbole. It does not use understatement, a comparison with 'like' or 'as', or the substitution of a related name.

questions.passage: Adaeze set the last solar panel on the roof of her mother's shop and wiped her hands on her wrapper. For three weeks, the twelve-year-old had collected discarded phone batteries, tested them with a borrowed meter and drawn coils of copper wire on the back of an old calendar. Now the small box beside the cooler hummed. Her mother's customers, who had laughed when she first called it a 'sun bank', began to bring their phones. Adaeze did not smile; she watched the red light on the box as if it might change its mind. When the first phone beeped, she let out a breath she had not known she was holding. That evening, the tailor from the next street asked if she could build one for his shop too. She looked at the empty battery shells on the floor and said, 'Only if you bring your own old phones.'
questions.q: The tailor's request and Adaeze's reply at the end of the passage chiefly serve to
options: prove that the invention has failed to attract ordinary customers
introduce a romance that will dominate the rest of the story
show that local interest has begun to grow and that Adaeze is practical about expanding her work
create comic relief after a scene of great danger
questions.explanation: The tailor asks for a similar device, which marks a small turning point after the first phone beeps, and Adaeze's condition about old phones reveals her practical, resourceful character. There is no romantic plot, comic relief, or evidence of failure in the passage.

questions.passage:
At the table where our father says grace,
five faces fall into their private light.
The rice goes cold; the stew keeps its slow
red counsel. Mother's spoon taps once,
then again, as if to call the room
back from a country with no roads.
Under the silence a small phone hums,
a beetle trapped in a glass jar.
Father clears his throat. Nobody looks up.
The salt sits midway, waiting for a hand.
questions.q: The image 'five faces fall into their private light' chiefly conveys that each person at the table is
options: ashamed to look at the father
absorbed in the glow of a personal screen rather than the shared meal
turning toward the window for daylight
questions.explanation: The 'private light' suggests the separate glow of phone screens, and the falling faces show the family withdrawing from one another. Nothing in the line suggests prayer, shame, or a turn toward the window.

questions.q: The overall tone of the poem is best described as
questions.explanation: The cold rice, the silence, and the line 'Nobody looks up' present the family's absorption in their phones critically, but the language remains quiet and controlled. This makes the tone restrained disapproval rather than celebration, amusement, or rage.

questions.passage: At exactly seven, Mama Ngozi set the pot of ofe nsala on the centre table. The children had washed their hands twice, but they waited, eyes on the lid, while she counted the pieces of chicken. There were six pieces and seven people. She lifted the smallest piece onto Chidi's plate and pushed the largest towards Papa. 'Eat slowly,' she said, though no one had spoken. Chidi turned his meat over with his spoon, measuring it, then quietly slid it onto his younger sister's plate. Papa saw, but continued to chew, staring at the wall as if the plaster held news. When the pot was empty, Mama Ngozi stacked the plates, and the clatter sounded louder than it should in a room where everyone had eaten.
questions.q: The final sentence, 'the clatter sounded louder than it should in a room where everyone had eaten', chiefly conveys...
options: a tense silence beneath the family's attempt to behave normally
that the plates and spoons were of poor quality
that Mama Ngozi regretted giving Papa the largest piece
that the family was still hungry after the meal
questions.explanation: After Chidi quietly gives away his meat and Papa stares at the wall, no one speaks. The ordinary sound of stacked plates seems loud because the silence and restraint in the room make it conspicuous. The statement that everyone had eaten also rules out simple hunger as the cause.

questions.q: During a moonlight storytelling in Makurdi, the narrator sings a line and the listeners answer in chorus. This technique is chiefly used to...
options: mark the exact moment when the story ends
provide a written record of the story
allow the narrator to change the plot without notice
draw the audience into the performance and keep them attentive
questions.explanation: The call-and-response exchange makes listeners active participants and helps sustain attention during the performance. It is not a way of recording the tale in writing, nor is it mainly a signal that the story has ended. In oral performance, audience response is part of the art itself.

questions.q: A line or phrase repeated at regular intervals in a poem, often at the end of stanzas, is called a...
questions.explanation: A refrain is a repeated line or phrase that returns at planned points in a poem or song. Its repetition can build rhythm or emphasize theme. A sonnet is a fixed-form poem, an epigram is a short witty saying, and a stanza is a verse paragraph.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The old tarred road embraced the new culvert at the village entrance,' the figure of speech used is
questions.explanation: The road is given the human action of embracing, which is personification. A simile would require an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as', while hyperbole would be deliberate exaggeration.

questions.passage: At dawn, Alhaji Musa stood at the edge of the dried pond in Dutsin-Ma and counted the jerrycans lined up like patient mourners. Behind him, his daughter Fatima pressed a naira note into the water seller's palm, but the man shook his head as though the money had suddenly become stones. The sun climbed. Women scraped the sandy bed with calabashes, and boys dug small holes that filled with muddy water and died before noon. Musa said nothing. In his mind he heard the voice of the village head from the previous night: 'We shall pray for rain, but we must also dig.' The last jerrycan was sold before the first cock crowed.
questions.q: The sentence 'In his mind he heard the voice of the village head from the previous night' mainly serves to
options: reveal Musa's inner reflection and link the present water shortage to earlier counsel
show that the village head is physically present at the pond
suggest that Musa has forgotten the village head's warning
introduce a direct conversation between Musa and Fatima
questions.explanation: The sentence takes the reader into Musa's thoughts and recalls the village head's earlier advice about prayer and digging. It does not present a present conversation or indicate that the village head is at the pond.

questions.passage: At dawn, Alhaji Musa stood at the edge of the dried pond in Dutsin-Ma and counted the jerrycans lined up like patient mourners. Behind him, his daughter Fatima pressed a naira note into the water seller's palm, but the man shook his head as though the money had suddenly become stones. The sun climbed. Women scraped the sandy bed with calabashes, and boys dug small holes that filled with muddy water and died before noon. Musa said nothing. In his mind he heard the voice of the village head from the previous night: 'We shall pray for rain, but we must also dig.' The last jerrycan was sold before the first cock crowed.
questions.q: The description of the women scraping the sandy bed and the boys digging holes that 'died before noon' mainly conveys the villagers'
options: desperate and largely futile search for water
confidence that rain will fall at noon
questions.explanation: The women and boys are struggling to find water in a dried pond, and the holes dying before noon show that their efforts are quickly frustrated. The details present hardship rather than fishing, indifference, or confidence in coming rain.

questions.passage:
The mould was a quiet tenant on the dish,
a blue-green stranger the scientist had not invited.
For days the bacteria multiplied like gossip in a market,
until a pale halo appeared where the stranger fed—
a ring of silence in the crowded plate.
He did not throw the spoiled culture away.
He bent, patient as a farmer reading an unripe sky,
and learned that some things kill by making room.
The world would later call it medicine;
that morning it was only a curious stain
on a bench in London, and a man
who chose to look twice.
questions.q: The phrase 'a ring of silence in the crowded plate' chiefly describes
options: a literal bell that rang in the laboratory
the scientist's refusal to speak during the experiment
the clear area where the mould had stopped the bacteria from growing
the crowded market outside the laboratory
questions.explanation: The phrase is a figurative description of the clear zone around the mould in a plate crowded with bacteria. It does not refer to an actual bell or to the scientist's silence.

questions.q: The comparison of the bacteria to 'gossip in a market' mainly emphasizes their
questions.explanation: Gossip in a market spreads quickly and reaches many people, so the simile emphasizes how fast and widely the bacteria multiplied. The comparison is not about their commercial value or friendliness.

questions.q: The line 'a man / who chose to look twice' chiefly suggests that the discovery depended on
options: the scientist's fear of spoiled cultures
the immediate support of the government
close and patient observation of an unexpected result
questions.explanation: The phrase shows that the scientist paid careful attention to a strange result instead of ignoring it. The poem stresses patient observation, not expensive equipment or government support.

questions.passage: At the assembly ground on Monday, Ifeoma did not begin with the usual greetings. She held up a small, cracked calculator that had served her through three terms and asked whether it was less useful than a tablet. The new rule said every student must buy the official learning tablet from one shop at ₦45,000. She reminded the principal that many parents in Unguwar Sani sold vegetables to pay school fees. Her voice was calm, but her words fell like stones into a basin of water, each one sending rings through the silent crowd. When she sat down, the senior prefect's clap started slowly, then spread across the compound like harmattan fire in dry grass.
questions.q: The comparison of Ifeoma's words to stones dropped into a basin of water chiefly suggests that her words
options: were heavy and difficult for the students to understand
were quiet at first but produced a wide and lasting effect
made the crowd angry and noisy
sounded sweet and pleasing to the principal
questions.explanation: The image shows a calm statement creating rings through a silent crowd, so the effect is quiet but spreading. It does not suggest confusion, anger, or sweetness.

questions.passage: At the assembly ground on Monday, Ifeoma did not begin with the usual greetings. She held up a small, cracked calculator that had served her through three terms and asked whether it was less useful than a tablet. The new rule said every student must buy the official learning tablet from one shop at ₦45,000. She reminded the principal that many parents in Unguwar Sani sold vegetables to pay school fees. Her voice was calm, but her words fell like stones into a basin of water, each one sending rings through the silent crowd. When she sat down, the senior prefect's clap started slowly, then spread across the compound like harmattan fire in dry grass.
questions.q: What is Ifeoma's main argument against the new rule?
options: It allows only the senior prefect to speak at assembly.
It forbids students from using calculators during lessons.
It obliges parents to buy an expensive tablet from a single shop.
It requires every student to sell vegetables to pay school fees.
questions.explanation: Ifeoma contrasts her cheap calculator with the compulsory ₦45,000 tablet that must be bought from one shop. The vegetable-selling detail supports her concern about cost, but it is not the rule itself.

questions.passage: At the assembly ground on Monday, Ifeoma did not begin with the usual greetings. She held up a small, cracked calculator that had served her through three terms and asked whether it was less useful than a tablet. The new rule said every student must buy the official learning tablet from one shop at ₦45,000. She reminded the principal that many parents in Unguwar Sani sold vegetables to pay school fees. Her voice was calm, but her words fell like stones into a basin of water, each one sending rings through the silent crowd. When she sat down, the senior prefect's clap started slowly, then spread across the compound like harmattan fire in dry grass.
questions.q: The comparison of the applause to 'harmattan fire in dry grass' mainly conveys that the applause
options: was impossible to control and very dangerous
questions.explanation: Fire in dry grass spreads quickly, and the clause describes the clap spreading across the compound. The image emphasises speed and spread, not literal danger or lack of enthusiasm.

questions.passage:
At early dawn the people came,
With patient feet and hopeful eyes;
They wrote their names and spoke their aim
Beneath the wide and waking skies.
The ballot box, a quiet drum,
Received each folded paper voice;
The elders watched, the children hummed,
And every voter made a choice.
questions.q: In each stanza, the first and third lines rhyme while the second and fourth lines rhyme. This arrangement is best described as
questions.explanation: The rhyme moves between two sets of lines in alternation, as in came/aim and eyes/skies. Enclosed rhyme follows an ABBA pattern, couplet rhyme uses successive pairs, and blank verse is unrhymed.

questions.passage:
At early dawn the people came,
With patient feet and hopeful eyes;
They wrote their names and spoke their aim
Beneath the wide and waking skies.
The ballot box, a quiet drum,
Received each folded paper voice;
The elders watched, the children hummed,
And every voter made a choice.
questions.q: The rising rhythm of the poem is created mainly by feet in which each unit consists of
options: an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable
a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable
two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable
questions.explanation: The lines move from unstressed to stressed syllables, producing an iambic rising rhythm. A stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one would create a falling rhythm, not the pattern heard here.

questions.q: In the performance of a folktale, the audience's clapping or answering 'Ee!' at intervals mainly serves to
options: replace the use of proverbs in the story
show that the audience is taking part in the performance
allow the narrator to forget the next part
prove that the story is historically true
questions.explanation: African oral literature is participatory, and audience responses encourage the narrator and mark involvement. They do not prove historical truth, help the narrator forget, or replace proverbs.

questions.q: Riddles are commonly used in African oral literature mainly to
options: sharpen wit and observation while entertaining the audience
teach children to avoid asking questions
record the exact date of an event
questions.explanation: Riddles are a mental game that trains attention, reasoning and imagination within an entertaining setting. Their main purpose is not historical dating, silencing questions, or replacing funeral songs.

questions.q: A writer's use of a mild or indirect expression in place of one that may seem harsh is called
questions.explanation: Euphemism softens an unpleasant or harsh idea, as in saying 'passed away' for 'died'. Litotes is understatement by negation, while hyperbole and oxymoron involve exaggeration and contradictory terms.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The harmattan wrote its signature on every lip in the village,' the figure of speech used is...
questions.explanation: The harmattan is given the human act of writing a signature, so it is personified. A simile would require an explicit comparison using like or as.

questions.q: In 'The ministry sent a new pen to inspect the clinic,' the expression 'a new pen' is used as...
questions.explanation: The pen stands for the official who uses it, by association, making the expression metonymic. An oxymoron joins contradictory terms, while an apostrophe addresses an absent or non-human entity.

questions.passage: Mrs Okafor set her megaphone on the bench and looked at the traders who had gathered in Ose Market. She knew what they had been told: that the cholera vaccine was a plot to reduce their children's strength. She did not mention the vaccine at first. Instead she asked who remembered little Ada, the vegetable seller's daughter who had died after drinking from the stream. A man in a faded Arsenal shirt, who doubted every new thing from the government, feared that the health workers would demand money before they began. He asked about the fee. Mrs Okafor opened her bag, showed the free vials, and said the only payment was clean hands and boiled water. At noon, the same man removed his cap and was the first to roll up his sleeve.
questions.q: The detail that the man in the faded Arsenal shirt later removes his cap and rolls up his sleeve mainly serves to...
options: interrupt the narrative with an unrelated comic incident
reveal that the health workers have bribed the man
introduce a new conflict between the traders
show the campaign's effect through a change in a sceptical character's action
questions.explanation: His change from doubt to willingness is shown through action, not direct explanation, and this indirectly confirms that Mrs Okafor has persuaded the crowd. The passage gives no evidence of bribery or an unrelated comic interruption.

questions.passage:
The Forest Keeps No Receipt
The forest keeps no receipt for the trees
we took; no ledger for the horn
that left the antelope's skull to the sun.
At dusk the ranger walks his line of wire,
his torch a thin argument against the dark.
He hears the generators of logging camps
humming like mosquitoes in a wound.
In the morning the schoolchildren come
with seedlings wrapped in old newspaper,
and their small hands press promises into soil.
Later the rain will count each leaf
as if the earth had learned arithmetic.
But the forest keeps no receipt,
only the long debt of smoke.
questions.q: The phrase 'his torch a thin argument against the dark' chiefly suggests that the ranger's effort is...
options: a useless gesture that changes nothing
frail but meaningful resistance to destruction
a secret signal to the logging camps
questions.explanation: 'Thin' makes the torchlight seem weak, but 'against the dark' gives it a purpose of resistance. Calling it useless overlooks the value the poem gives to the ranger's effort.

questions.passage:
The Forest Keeps No Receipt
The forest keeps no receipt for the trees
we took; no ledger for the horn
that left the antelope's skull to the sun.
At dusk the ranger walks his line of wire,
his torch a thin argument against the dark.
He hears the generators of logging camps
humming like mosquitoes in a wound.
In the morning the schoolchildren come
with seedlings wrapped in old newspaper,
and their small hands press promises into soil.
Later the rain will count each leaf
as if the earth had learned arithmetic.
But the forest keeps no receipt,
only the long debt of smoke.
questions.q: The comparison of the generators to 'mosquitoes in a wound' mainly conveys that the logging...
options: is a persistent and harmful activity that feeds on damage
is a small and harmless nuisance
questions.explanation: Mosquitoes around a wound suggest irritation, persistence and infection, so the generators image presents logging as harmful. The simile does not suggest healing or control by the children.

questions.q: The overall tone of the poem is best described as...
options: sombre with a note of hope
questions.explanation: The loss of trees, the antelope's skull and the 'long debt of smoke' create a sombre tone, while the seedlings and the rain counting leaves offer a cautious hope. The poem is not light-hearted, purely celebratory or emotionally detached.

questions.passage: The bus left Onitsha before dawn, its headlamps cutting two weak tunnels through the rain. Adaeze sat by the window with a plastic bag of oranges on her lap and a brown envelope pinned inside her wrapper. She was travelling to Sokoto to see her brother, who had written that the mechanic apprenticeship was finally paying. At Asaba, the driver stopped to bargain with a man selling boiled eggs; by Lokoja, the wipers had begun to screech. When the bus broke down near Okene, the passengers stood in a ring under the mango trees while the conductor counted naira notes and the mechanic spoke of a part that 'only God can find.' Adaeze held her envelope tighter. In the late afternoon, a lorry carrying yams overtook them, and she watched the yams bounce like brown fists against the tar. When the bus finally coughed to life, the old woman beside her said, 'A road that refuses to end still reaches somewhere.' Adaeze smiled, though she did not understand why.
questions.q: When the bus breaks down, Adaeze holds her envelope tighter. This action chiefly shows that the breakdown
options: proves that she has lost her brother's address
makes her angry with the conductor
makes her more anxious about keeping the envelope's contents safe
persuades her to abandon the journey
questions.explanation: The tightening grip on the envelope is a response to the delay and uncertainty of the breakdown, showing concern for what she is carrying. It does not show anger at the conductor or loss of the address. The action reveals anxiety about safety and security.

questions.q: The simile 'the yams bounce like brown fists against the tar' chiefly emphasizes the
options: forceful, jolting movement of the yams on the road
questions.explanation: The comparison to 'brown fists' suggests repeated hard impact as the yams strike the tar. It is mainly about rough movement and force, not merely colour or the passengers' hunger. The lorry's speed is less important than the violent bouncing.

questions.q: The old woman's statement, 'A road that refuses to end still reaches somewhere,' chiefly serves to
options: criticize the driver for taking a wrong route
show that the old woman is tired of travelling
warn Adaeze that another breakdown is coming

questions.explanation: The remark is a consoling, proverb-like comment made after a difficult delay, suggesting that even a long road has a destination. It is not a warning about another breakdown or a direct criticism of the driver. Its main function is to offer encouragement.

questions.q: A praise singer in a traditional African community is important mainly because the singer
options: settles land disputes before the elders
teaches children how to read and write
keeps alive the people's history and the memory of heroic deeds
controls the coming of rain for the new year
questions.explanation: Praise singers preserve genealogies, histories and the reputation of leaders and heroes through recitation and song. Their role is not primarily formal education, dispute settlement or rainmaking. They function as living archives of communal memory.

questions.passage:
The wind is cold, the moon is high,
The fishing boats go out to sea;
The young men row and do not cry,
And sing to keep their spirits free.

The nets are heavy, dark and wide,
The tide is rising on the shore;
The tired men with weary pride
Count silver fish and ask for more.
questions.q: The line 'The wind is cold, the moon is high' consists of four metrical feet, each formed by an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable. The metre is
questions.explanation: A foot of one unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable is an iamb, and four such feet make tetrameter. The line scans as an unstressed-stressed pattern four times. Trochaic metre would reverse the pattern, while pentameter would require five feet.
